Hi Olivia / Raj —

Quick recap from our call today + next steps so we have a single place to track actions:

1) Integration & auth
   - SDK setup: you plan to use the Node SDK for generation + embeddings. Aditya will share the exact code snippets and an example repo.
   - Auth: FinTechCo prefers IP-restricted API keys behind the VPC private control plane. We verified Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS for key rotation.

2) Routing & model variants
   - You want routing by workload (low-latency chat vs. high-throughput embeddings/rerank). We recommended keeping two model variants: a low-latency generate model and a quantized reranker/embedding model.

3) Structured output / tool calling
   - For structured output & function/tool-calling, enable the "function calls" mode in the SDK; ensure your schema is validated at the application layer.

4) Embeddings / rerankers
   - We recommend async batch embeddings for indexing (to smooth throughput) + a synchronous re-ranker for top-N when latency requirement is <300ms p95. If re-ranking at very low p95 is required, we can route to a more powerful GPU pool.

5) Dedicated capacity sizing & autoscaling (open items)
   - Ask: can you confirm typical qps, average tokens per request, and peak concurrent requests? We need these to propose nodes and queue sizing.
   - Initial suggestion: start with a small pool (2-3 nodes) with aggressive autoscale to handle spikes; tune concurrency and queue depth per model.

Attachments: integration-checklist.pdf (integration items), I'll follow up with our sizing workbook (redwood-dedicated-sizing.xlsx).

Hi all — tagging in some concrete recommendations based on Olivia's numbers. High level answers to Olivia's question below, plus the sizing assumptions I used (see attached workbook).

1) GPU vs CPU for rerankers\   - For top-50 reranking at p95 <450ms, GPU is strongly recommended if the model is transformer-based and you do full forward passes per candidate. CPU can work if you switch to a lighter-weight cross-encoder or use quantized/optimized CPU runtimes, but p95 will be higher and costs may be unpredictable under spike load.

2) Concurrency limits & per-GPU throughput\   - On recent A100/H100-class instances with optimized kernels we see ~100–160 concurrent small-generation requests per GPU (for low-latency models) and ~200–300 embedding ops per GPU when batched. For rerankers doing 50 forward passes, estimate ~15–30 concurrent rerank requests per GPU depending on model size and quantization.

3) Autoscale policy suggestions\   - Min nodes: 2 (warm pool)
   - Target utilization: 60–70% GPU utilization
   - Scale step: +1 node when queue depth > 25 for > 30s; scale down when utilization < 30% for 3m (graceful cool-down)
   - Queue depth: configure request queue with a max wait of 1.2s for user-facing flows; background batch jobs should run on a separate queue with larger depth and pre-warmed workers.

4) Queueing & routing
   - Separate queues by workload: "interactive" (low latency, small batch size), "embedding-batch" (large batched jobs), and "rerank-sync" (synchronous top-N reranks). Use routing policies to send requests to the correct GPU pool/variant.

5) Example sizing (based on your peak 650 qps):
   - If generation avg 450 tokens and we assume ~20 tokens/sec throughput per token GPU for the chosen model, estimate 3–4 GPUs for low-latency generation plus 2 GPUs for reranking (quantized) to meet p95 targets with autoscale buffer. This is a rough starting point — workbook attached has adjustable parameters.

Attachments: redwood-dedicated-sizing.xlsx (workbook with model-by-model assumptions and node estimates).

Next steps: I can present the workbook in the tech deep-dive tomorrow; if you can share a representative request trace (timestamps, tokens/request) even better — we'll plug it into the model.
